archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A Burrow-driven offense that throws more than any team in the league over expectation, paired with a defense whose pass rush has dragged it from the bottom of the league back to the middle, good enough to win most weeks but not yet clean enough to dominate.

report.headline: A real playoff-caliber team, but its run defense keeps leaking.
report.take:
Cincinnati is exactly what its 3-2 record says, and a little better. Wins over expected sits at essentially zero, the point differential implies three wins, and the net EPA ranks 7th. Nothing here is a mirage built on coin-flip finishes. This is a team that has earned its record and has played closer to the top ten than the bottom of a crowded AFC North, where it currently sits last only because everyone else has played one more game.

The identity is unmistakable. The Bengals lead the league in pass rate over expected, and Joe Burrow has started every game and owns the offense. Tee Higgins, not Ja'Marr Chase, leads the team in targets, with Chase Brown a real third option out of the backfield. The line's raw protection numbers are poor: pressure allowed ranks 26th. Burrow neutralizes that by getting the ball out fast, and the sack rate ranks 7th. The run game is efficient at not losing yards, with the 2nd-best stuff rate and 2nd-best short-yardage conversion, but it rarely creates anything, at 3.65 yards a carry. The other half of the turnaround is the defense. Last year's unit ranked 29th in EPA allowed. This one is 15th, and the pass rush, 4th in pressure rate and 3rd in sack rate, is the reason.

What the averages hide is a defense with two personalities. Against the pass, and especially deep, it is good. Against the run and in the short area it is among the worst in football: 28th in rush EPA allowed, 30th in explosive runs allowed, 29th on short passes, 27th in missed tackles and 29th on third down. It has survived because offenses stall inside the 20, where its red-zone TD rate ranks 4th, and because takeaways came in bunches against Tampa Bay and Miami. Red-zone stands and turnover bursts are the two things most likely to regress. If they do and the tackling doesn't improve, the points allowed will climb.

The outlook is still good. The remaining schedule is soft: Tennessee, Atlanta, Washington, New Orleans and Indianapolis all have losing records. The offense is efficient enough to carry the team through weeks when the defense bends. The ceiling depends on whether the run defense can hold up in a division full of physical games.

strengths.title: A pass rush that lives in backfields
strengths.body: The front ranks 4th in pressure rate and 3rd in sack rate, and it had three or more sacks in four of five games. This is the biggest single change from a 2025 defense that ranked 29th in EPA allowed. Pressure is the stickiest defensive trait, so this should hold, and it explains why the deep pass defense ranks 5th.

strengths.title: Burrow's quick-trigger aerial offense
strengths.body: No team throws more than expected, and the passing game ranks 12th in EPA while overall success rate ranks 8th. A fast release turns a line that allows pressure at a 26th-ranked rate into one that allows sacks at a 7th-ranked rate. With Burrow healthy and two lead receivers sharing the load, this is the engine and it travels.

strengths.title: Winning the critical yard
strengths.body: The offense converts short yardage at the league's 2nd-best rate and gets stuffed less than all but one team. That keeps drives alive even though the run game creates few chunk plays. On defense, the 4th-ranked red-zone TD rate has turned long drives into field goals.

concerns.title: Run defense gives up chunks
concerns.body: This defense ranks 28th in rush EPA allowed and 30th in explosive runs allowed, and Miami ran for 217 yards in Week 5. It is a real structural flaw, not noise. Missed tackles rank 27th, and the short-pass defense (29th) shows the same problem in space. An aggressive, rush-first front can leave lanes behind it, and the remaining division schedule will test it.

concerns.title: Third downs and red-zone luck
concerns.body: Opponents convert third downs at the 4th-highest rate in the league, yet the red zone ranks 4th in TD rate. That combination usually doesn't last. Bending this much and still not breaking near the goal line tends to regress, and when it does, the 14th-ranked scoring defense will look worse.

concerns.title: Penalties and a one-note ground game
concerns.body: At 8 penalties a game (24th), the Bengals hand drives away. The Week 4 loss to Jacksonville came with 108 penalty yards and only 23 rushing yards, despite 428 through the air. The run game averages 3.65 a carry (20th), so when the passing game stalls there is little to lean on.

trend.note: Two wins, two losses, then a win at Miami. The passing game has swung from negative EPA in the first two weeks to strongly positive since. The defense has either forced turnovers in bunches or forced none, so week-to-week results have tracked those swings more than any steady climb.

nextGame.headline: Rested Bengals catch Baltimore without its starting quarterback and center
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati comes off its bye to visit Baltimore as a 2.5-point underdog with a 51.5 total, in a game that decides who climbs out of a four-way AFC North scramble. Stylistically it is a clean contrast. The Bengals pass more than anyone over expectation. Baltimore runs well (4.61 a carry, 4th) and is 26th in pass rate over expected. The Ravens' defense is stout underneath, ranking 4th on short passes, but leaky deep (22nd) and to opposing WR1s, where it ranks 31st in EPA allowed. It also generates little pressure (24th).

Availability tilts the matchup. Lamar Jackson is listed out with an ankle sprain after Tyler Huntley started the last two games, including a 13-10 loss to Cleveland. The coach calls Jackson day-to-day with a chance to practice, so his status is the swing of the week. Baltimore is also without its every-down center Cam Jurgens, plus guard Andrew Vorhees and tight end Matt Hibner, and Rashod Bateman is questionable but expected to be OK. Cincinnati's own report is light: safety Kyle Dugger and receiver Colbie Young are questionable in limited roles, and backup tight end Tanner Hudson is on IR.

waysToWin.title: Higgins and Chase attack Baltimore deep
waysToWin.body: Baltimore's defense is stingy on short throws but ranks 22nd on deep passes and 31st in EPA allowed to WR1s. Higgins leads the Bengals in targets and Chase is right behind him. Burrow has to push the ball downfield rather than live in the quick game, which plays straight into Baltimore's strength underneath.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush vs a patched line
waysToWin.body: The Bengals' 4th-ranked pressure rate meets a Ravens line that already allows sacks at a 22nd-ranked rate and is now missing its starting center and a guard. If Huntley starts, a backup quarterback behind a reshuffled interior is the matchup this front was built to exploit.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yards
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati ranks 12th in special-teams EPA per game, while Baltimore's is negative and ranks 23rd. The Bengals also rank 6th in turnover differential per game, against a Ravens defense 22nd in takeaways. In a game priced under a field goal, field position and a takeaway could decide it.

waysToLose.title: Baltimore runs right through them
waysToLose.body: This is the matchup that most favors the Ravens. Their efficient, run-leaning offense faces a Bengals defense 28th in rush EPA allowed and 30th in explosive runs. If Baltimore stays ahead of the chains on the ground, it shortens the game and keeps Burrow off the field, regardless of who plays quarterback.

waysToLose.title: Quick game smothered underneath
waysToLose.body: Burrow gets rid of the ball faster than almost anyone. Baltimore's 4th-ranked defense against short passes is built to eat exactly those throws. If the Ravens take away the underneath game and the run game can't punish them at 3.65 a carry, drives stall.

waysToLose.title: Lamar plays and third downs leak
waysToLose.body: Jackson is listed out but could practice. If he plays, Baltimore's 6th-ranked passing offense pairs with the scramble threat against a defense that allows third-down conversions at the 4th-highest rate. Long drives that extend on third down would test the red-zone defense more than it can likely withstand.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lamar Jackson practices this week. With him this is a coin-flip shootout, and with Huntley behind a line missing its center, the Bengals' pass rush becomes the most important unit on the field.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable part. Burrow's efficiency, the pass-first approach and the quick release that masks the line should keep Cincinnati around the top ten in scoring, and the schedule after Baltimore is generous: Tennessee at home, then Atlanta, Washington, New Orleans and Indianapolis, all with losing records. The pass rush should travel too, and it is the main reason this defense will not return to last year's depths.

What likely regresses is the defense's finishing. A unit this porous on third down and against the run won't keep holding red-zone touchdowns at a top-five rate, and multi-takeaway games aren't bankable. Expect points allowed to drift up a little, with the offense still carrying the team to a winning record. The division games against Pittsburgh, Cleveland twice and Baltimore again, plus Kansas City at home, will decide whether that means a wild card or a title.
swingFactors: Run defense and tackling vs physical division opponents
Burrow's health behind a line that allows pressure
Whether takeaways and red-zone stops hold up

confidence.note: Five games and a stable QB, but the defense's splits are extreme and partly built on turnover bursts.
